criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Memo identifies ELUR conflict with ground-floor residential use
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly flags the ELUR conflict. Part IV.G.1 states that the ELUR prohibits residential use on the ground floor and defines 'residential use' broadly, while Term Sheet §4(a) contemplates 'ground-floor residential lobby and amenity spaces (fitness centre, package room, resident lounge, and leasing office),' noting that 'the Term Sheet describes a building the ELUR may prohibit.' The ELUR is identified by recording reference (Vol. 412, Pg. 88) in Part II.2(c), the issue is ranked as risk #7 in the executive risk register, Halcyon's enforcement-exposure warning is quoted, and draft treatment (§§9.3(b)–(d), 2.5(l)) and residual risk are addressed.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Lease defines permitted residential use to exclude ground-floor habitable space
criteria_results.reasoning: The draft squarely addresses the ELUR ground-floor restriction. Section 9.3(a) distinguishes habitable residential space below grade (dwelling, sleeping, cooking, eating — prohibited by the ELUR) from non-habitable ancillary spaces such as lobbies, mail rooms, fitness centers, package rooms, resident lounges, and leasing offices, which the ELUR does not expressly address. Section 9.3(b) obligates Landlord to obtain a DEEP interpretation/variance confirming the permissibility of ground-floor lobby/amenity uses, and Section 9.3(c) provides that pending that confirmation Tenant will locate dwelling units on floors 2 and above and limit ground-floor uses to retail, commercial, mechanical, parking, and other clearly non-habitable functions. Section 9.3(e) and Section 11.5(d) further require all affordable units to be located above the ground floor consistent with the ELUR. The lease therefore both distinguishes habitable from non-habitable ground-floor space and restricts dwelling units to upper floors to comply with the ELUR, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Affordable housing units specified for upper floors only
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly requires upper-floor placement of affordable units in connection with the ELUR ground-floor residential restriction. Section 9.3(e) ('Affordable Units Placement') states that 'Tenant shall locate all affordable housing units on floors above the ground floor, consistent with the ELUR and the recommendations in the Phase II Environmental Site Assessment, and the Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreement shall so provide.' Section 11.5(d)(i) repeats that affordable housing units shall be 'located on floors above the ground floor, consistent with the ELUR and Section 9.3(e),' and Exhibit K likewise specifies 'upper-floor placement consistent with the ELUR.' The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Memo identifies mechanics' lien as title defect requiring resolution
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo contains a dedicated section (Part IV.M, 'The Mechanics' Lien — A Direct Conflict Between Two of Your Sources') that expressly identifies the Calloway Marine Demolition Inc. mechanics' lien in the amount of $187,500, filed April 3, 2025 and recorded at Volume 418, Page 302. It frames the lien as a title defect: it notes the conflict between the Term Sheet (which lists the lien as a Permitted Exception) and Title Commitment Requirement No. 7 (which bars policy issuance until the requirement is satisfied), and it prescribes resolution — discharge, bonding under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37, or insuring over — as a Landlord obligation at Landlord's cost, made a condition precedent in §2.5(f) and expressly removed from the Permitted Exceptions in Exhibit C. It is also flagged in the critical-path table and the negotiation matrix. The criterion is therefore fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Lease requires Authority to discharge mechanics' lien as condition precedent or provides indemnity
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly allocates responsibility for the pre-existing Calloway Marine Demolition mechanics' lien to the Authority (Landlord) and makes clearing it a condition precedent to the Lease Commencement Date. Section 2.5(f) conditions commencement on Landlord delivering evidence that the Calloway Lien has been discharged of record, bonded over under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37, or insured over without exception (the 'Lien Condition'). Section 3.3(a) covenants Landlord to remove it at its sole cost, and Section 3.6 separately requires Landlord, at its sole cost, to discharge, bond over, or insure over the lien on or before the Lease Commencement Date and includes an indemnity running to Tenant and the Leasehold Mortgagee that survives termination. Section 3.1(c) also carves this out of the 'AS IS' acceptance, and Exhibit C expressly lists the lien as NOT a Permitted Exception that must be cleared before commencement. This satisfies the criterion on multiple independent grounds.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Memo identifies rent calculation rounding discrepancy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo's figure-reconciliation table does treat the per-SF rate, but it computes $2,850,000 ÷ 139,392 = $20.446 and marks the result '✓' (exact/consistent), expressly labeling $20.45/SF as approximate. It never performs or flags the reverse calculation ($20.45 × 139,392 ≈ $2,850,566), never identifies the ~$566 rounding gap between the per-SF rate and the stated $2,850,000 annual lump sum, and never discusses which figure controls. The only discrepancy the memo calls out in base rent is the Year-16 reset cliff (Part IV.F). Thus the specific discrepancy required by ISSUE_003 is not identified.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Lease specifies which rent figure controls (lump sum vs. per-SF rate)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.2 fixes the initial annual Base Rent at $2,850,000 (monthly $237,500) as the operative covenant, and merely 'acknowledges' that this figure 'equates to approximately $20.45 per square foot.' The per-SF rate is expressly framed as approximate/derivative of the controlling annual lump sum, and Section 2.2(b) further confirms the deemed square footage is used only for computing the per-SF equivalent with no rent adjustment. Thus the lease makes clear which figure controls, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Memo identifies conflict between reverter right and lender security interest
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the conflict between the reverter/forfeiture and Bayside's lender protections. Risk Register item #4 notes the reverter "is also Bayside's stated deal-breaker." Part IV.B.2 states the financing argument: "Bayside has said it will not lend against the provision as written." Part IV.C.2 explains that the Term Sheet's New Lease right "loses the right entirely on a reverter termination or a bankruptcy rejection — the two scenarios in which the lender most needs it," and notes Draft Lease §17.5 extends the New Lease to a Reverter Termination. IV.C.3 addresses the absence of lender cure rights for milestone defaults. Part IV.C.4 ties the reverter to the $380M appraised-value/LTV condition, and the Priority 2 table and §5.4 (mortgagee cure as hard prerequisite to reverter) reinforce that an unmodified reverter would render the $285M loan unfinanceable.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Lease subordinates reverter right to leasehold mortgage/lender protections
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output contains extensive protections subordinating the reverter right to leasehold mortgagee interests. Article 5.1(d) makes expiration of the Mortgagee Cure Period a condition precedent to any Reverter Termination. Section 5.4 requires simultaneous notice of any Milestone Default Notice to each Leasehold Mortgagee, grants the lender an independent 180-day cure period running consecutively (not concurrently) with Tenant's cure period, permits cure by any means including installing a replacement developer, states that termination before exhaustion of the Mortgagee Cure Period is void, and bars exercise of the reverter without the mortgagee's consent where the mortgagee has given notice of intent to exercise rights. Section 17.5 grants the Leasehold Mortgagee a New Lease right following any termination 'for any reason whatsoever — including ... a Reverter Termination,' and Section 17.6 reinforces cure rights for monetary, non-monetary, and milestone defaults, including post-foreclosure cure. Section 5.5(b) also floors Improvement Compensation at the outstanding Indebtedness, and Section 5.9 requires mediation before exercise. These squarely satisfy every example in the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Memo identifies conflict between ROFR and lender foreclosure rights
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the conflict: it flags the recorded Right of First Refusal as lacking a foreclosure/mortgagee carve-out, states that Bayside requires the unconditional right to foreclose and assign the lease to a qualified transferee without Landlord consent, and explains that lease provisions cannot cure the recorded instrument. It also ties this to Term Sheet §11's ROFR on assignments to non-affiliates during the first 20 years and lists the conflict in the risk register, detailed analysis, and negotiation matrix.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Lease carves out lender foreclosure/transfers from ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly carves out lender foreclosure and related transfers from the Authority's right of first refusal. Section 18.5(d) states the ROFR 'shall not apply to, and shall be deemed waived with respect to, any Permitted Transfer, including without limitation any grant of a Leasehold Mortgage, any foreclosure, deed in lieu of foreclosure, or other exercise of remedies by a Leasehold Mortgagee, any assignment by a Leasehold Mortgagee or its designee.' Section 18.5(e) further provides the ROFR shall not apply to, delay, condition, or impair the granting, enforcement, or foreclosure of any Leasehold Mortgage, collateral assignments, pledges of ownership interests, or transfers in connection therewith. Section 18.3(c) classifies foreclosure, deed-in-lieu, and mortgagee transfers as Permitted Transfers not subject to consent or the ROFR, and Section 18.6 requires recording an amendment to the existing Recorded ROFR to incorporate these carve-outs as a condition to the Lease Commencement Date. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo identifies 12-month force majeure cap may be insufficient for coastal waterfront project
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses coastal/flood risk extensively (FEMA Flood Zone AE, the November 2024 nor'easter, the bulkhead, casualty restoration), but it never addresses a 12-month aggregate force majeure cap. The only force-majeure-related reference is in Part IV.B.3, describing 'Force Majeure and permitting extensions (18 months)' as part of the milestone cure architecture, which is not the same as analyzing the adequacy of a 12-month aggregate force majeure cap. Nowhere does the memo identify that a 12-month force majeure cap may be insufficient for a coastal construction project, nor does it recommend increasing an aggregate cap beyond 12 months. The specific issue in the criterion is not raised.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo recommends force majeure cover climate-related events
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses climate/flood risk only in the casualty, insurance, and site-design contexts — e.g., Flood Zone AE, the November 2024 nor'easter reaching 10.5 feet NAVD88 against a 12-foot BFE, NFIP maximum coverage limits (§14.1(d)), floodplain/freeboard design, and dewatering. Force majeure is mentioned only once, in Part IV.B.3(ii), as a source of schedule extensions ('Force Majeure and permitting extensions (18 months) and the environmental and coastal extensions'), with no recommendation that the force majeure clause be expanded to expressly cover hurricanes, storm surge, flooding, or other climate-related events. The memo nowhere recommends drafting climate-related force majeure language, so the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Memo identifies CPI rent reset gap period ambiguity
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses the base rent escalation and the Year 16 CPI reset, including the inconsistency between annual compounding and 5-year step implementation and the resulting 13.14% cliff. However, it does not identify the specific structural ambiguity that the term sheet is silent on what governs annual increases during the periods between CPI reset dates (e.g., Years 16–25). The memo addresses the reset formula and proposes a draft treatment, but it never flags the gap in the term sheet regarding intervening-year increases. Therefore, the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Lease specifies interim escalation mechanism between CPI resets
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease provides CPI reset formulas at Reset Dates (Rent Years 16, 26, etc.) and fixed step escalations for Rent Years 1–15, but it does not specify any interim escalation mechanism for the years between CPI reset dates. After Rent Year 15, the text resets rent only at each 10-year Reset Date and leaves Base Rent flat during the intervening years, without fixed annual increases or another specified interim escalation. This is precisely the failure mode described in the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Memo identifies that percentage rent breakpoint is not indexed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly raises the issue at multiple points: Risk Register item 10 flags that the $28,500,000 percentage-rent breakpoint is 'fixed at $28.5M for 99 years' with none of the indexation applied to other rent components; Part IV.E analyzes it in depth, calling the Breakpoint 'the single nominal number in a ninety-nine-year instrument,' quantifying erosion (roughly 4% of Gross Revenues by Year 96), and stating the participation 'would have become a 2% tax on nearly the entire revenue stream' — 'the permanent gross revenue tax you were worried about.' It also recommends a fix: Section 7.5 of the Draft Lease indexes the Breakpoint on each Reset Date using the same CPI fraction applied to base rent, with a floor at $28,500,000, and the negotiation matrix (item 9) lists the indexed breakpoint as a Tier A position.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Lease indexes or periodically resets the percentage rent breakpoint
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.5 ("Indexation of the Breakpoint") expressly provides a mechanism to adjust the $28,500,000 Gross Revenue Breakpoint over time: on each Reset Date (Rent Years 16, 26, 36, 46, 56, 66, 76, 86, and 96, as defined in Section 1.1), the Breakpoint is multiplied by the same CPI-based fraction used to adjust Base Rent under Section 6.5(b), subject to a $28,500,000 floor. Section 7.5 also states the purpose is to preserve the economic relationship between the Breakpoint and project revenues over the full 99-year Term, and Section 20.5 applies the same adjustment to the extension period. The Breakpoint is therefore not fixed for the entire term but is periodically reset/indexed, satisfying the criterion. (The mechanism ties the Breakpoint to the CPI-based component of the Base Rent reset rather than to the greater-of escalation, but it is still a periodic indexation mechanism, which the criterion permits.)

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Memo identifies tax abatement timing misalignment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies and quantifies the tax abatement timing misalignment. Part IV.D.1 states that Term Sheet §10 commences the 15-year abatement on the Lease Commencement Date (October 1, 2025) while Rent Commencement is 36 months later (October 1, 2028), and explains that during the three construction years Tenant would pay $1,546,375/year in taxes on a vacant lot actually assessed at $145,950 — an excess of $1,400,425/year, or $4,201,275 over three years — while also burning three years of the 15-year benefit before income begins. Part IV.I reinforces this by showing the conflicting 'Lease Year' definitions (rent measured from Rent Commencement, abatement from Lease Commencement) and describes the Draft Lease fix (Abatement Period starting at Rent Commencement Date, §8.6(b)). The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Lease specifies tax abatement commences upon Rent Commencement or first CO
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.6(b) expressly provides that the Abatement Period commences on the Rent Commencement Date and not the Lease Commencement Date, and Section 8.6(c) separately addresses the construction-period gap by requiring 100% assessment from Lease Commencement until the Rent Commencement Date. The Rent Commencement Date (Section 6.3) is defined as the earlier of 36 months after Lease Commencement or issuance of a CO for 100 residential units, tying the abatement to revenue generation. Section 2.5(h) additionally conditions commencement on a Tax Abatement Agreement effective as of the Rent Commencement Date, and Section 8.6(d)-(e) confirms calculation on actual assessments rather than the Lease Commencement Date. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Memo addresses unconscionability of improvement forfeiture under reverter
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo squarely addresses the unconscionability/disproportionality of the improvement forfeiture. Part IV.B describes the Term Sheet's reverter as extinguishing $200–300M of Improvements plus the $5.7M LOC 'without any payment, compensation, or reimbursement,' and performs a detailed legal analysis: penalty/liquidated damages doctrine (Restatement §356) explaining the forfeiture is 'grossly disproportionate' to the Authority's actual harm; Connecticut equitable relief from forfeiture (Vachon v. Tomascak, 207 Conn. 70 (1988)) and Restatement §229; and unconscionability (Restatement §208). It also recommends alternatives, drafting Article 5 to give Tenant an election between fair-market-value buyout of Improvements and reimbursement of unreimbursed hard/soft costs (with §5.11(d) fair-value backstop), and the Executive Summary and negotiation matrix (item #1) flag the provision as 'unconscionable as drafted' and Bayside's deal-breaker. All elements of the criterion are satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Lease mitigates improvement forfeiture with buyout or reimbursement
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 5 of the lease expressly mitigates forfeiture on reverter. Section 5.5 grants Tenant 'Improvement Compensation' equal to the greater of (at Tenant's election) the Appraised Value of the Improvements or Tenant's actual unreimbursed Hard Costs and Soft Costs (net of insurance and Landlord's documented damages), with a floor equal to the outstanding Indebtedness secured by the Leasehold Mortgage (up to Appraised Value). Section 5.6 establishes a detailed MAI appraisal procedure. Section 5.7 makes payment of Improvement Compensation in full a condition precedent to any effective Reverter Termination, and Section 5.8 bars forfeiture of Improvements on any termination other than natural expiration, and caps combined recovery. Section 5.11 confirms the compensation is not a penalty. The 'without payment' language in Section 20.2 applies only to expiration of the 99-year Term, not to reverter, so it does not undercut the mitigation. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Memo identifies missing estoppel certificate framework
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo nowhere addresses estoppel certificates. The term 'estoppel' does not appear in the document, and no section flags that neither the Term Sheet nor the Bayside loan term sheet contains an estoppel certificate framework — nor does it discuss the importance of estoppel certificates for refinancing a 99-year leasehold subject to a leasehold mortgage. The financeability analysis (Part IV.C) enumerates Bayside's seven Section 5 ground-lease requirements (mortgage consent, SNDA, New Lease, cure periods, foreclosure/assignment free of ROFR, etc.) but omits any estoppel obligation, and the negotiation matrix and open-items list are likewise silent on the issue. The criterion is therefore not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease includes estoppel certificate provision with specified timeframe
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes an estoppel certificate provision. Section 21.5 requires each Party (including the Authority as Landlord) to deliver an estoppel certificate substantially in the form of Exhibit G 'within ten (10) Business Days after request,' and further caps requests to twice per twelve months except in financings/sales. Section 17.4 separately obligates Landlord to execute estoppel certificates 'within ten (10) Business Days after request' in connection with any financing, refinancing, or sale of the leasehold estate. Both provisions specify a clear response timeframe (10 business days), which falls within the 15–30 day example window. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease estoppel provision includes deemed-approval mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: The estoppel certificate provisions (Sections 17.4 and 21.5 and Exhibit G) require delivery within a specified time but do not include any deemed-approval or deemed-confirmation mechanism if the Authority fails to respond. Therefore, the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Memo identifies lack of affordable housing implementation detail
criteria_results.reasoning: Part IV.J of the memo expressly identifies the gap: 'The recorded covenant has six acknowledged gaps,' listing that the 2019 Declaration does not specify how the 15% is calculated if the unit count changes, income verification and tenant qualification procedures, a monitoring/compliance/enforcement entity, consequences for non-compliance, unit distribution, and location restrictions. It also flags that the covenant is 15% of an undetermined unit count (TBD in the Lease) and discusses duration/LIHTC extended-use subsidy timelines and the 99-year versus 30-year issue. This squarely satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Lease includes substantive affordable housing compliance provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 11.5 of the lease contains substantive affordable housing provisions well beyond a bare restatement of the 15% requirement. It addresses: (a) calculation method — 15% of total residential dwelling units, rounded with one-half rounded up, with recalculation on unit-count changes and a 12-month conforming period; (b) income verification/eligibility — HUD/CHFA-consistent verification and qualification procedures plus annual compliance reporting; (c) monitoring mechanism — designation of the City's Office of Community Development as monitoring entity with inspection and enforcement authority; (d) consequences of non-compliance — remedies expressly limited to specific performance and monetary damages after notice and 90-day cure, with no re-entry or forfeiture; (e) duration/treatment of the affordable period — a defined 30-year Affordable Housing Period with an amendment to the recorded Declaration of Restrictive Covenants to conform it; and (f) incorporation of a separate regulatory agreement — Exhibit K, Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreement, cross-referenced and incorporated. Additional detail is supplied on unit distribution, upper-floor placement consistent with the ELUR, and LIHTC use. This readily satisfies the requirement that at least two enumerated implementation elements be addressed.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Landlord name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease's preamble and cover page identify the Landlord as "CITY OF PORT CALLOWAY REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, a public body corporate and politic organized and existing under the provisions of the Connecticut General Statutes, Section 8-125 et seq." This matches the criterion's required name and entity type exactly. The definition of "Authority," Section 21.1, and Recital B consistently affirm this identification.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Tenant name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease identifies the Tenant as 'MERIDIAN GATEWAY HOLDINGS LLC' and repeatedly states it is a Delaware limited liability company. The tenant name and entity type are correct.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct property address and APN
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly identifies the Premises in Recital A as located at "10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, Connecticut 06801" and as "Assessor's Parcel No. 127-003-0045." The same address and APN are repeated in Section 2.2 (Premises; Legal Description) and referenced in Exhibit A. Both required identifiers are present and consistent throughout the document.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct parcel size
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease repeatedly references the Premises as approximately 3.2 acres (139,392 square feet), including in Recital D, Section 2.2, and Exhibit A. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct lease term of 99 years from October 1, 2025
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 2.4 states a 99-year Term commencing October 1, 2025 (or later per conditions precedent) and expiring at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on September 30, 2124, which matches the required 99-year calculation from October 1, 2025.

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct initial annual base rent of $2,850,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.2 states initial annual Base Rent of $2,850,000, payable in equal monthly installments of $237,500, which matches the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct Rent Commencement Date definition
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.3 defines the Rent Commencement Date as the earlier of 36 months after the Lease Commencement Date and the date a temporary or permanent certificate of occupancy is first issued for at least 100 residential dwelling units within the Residential Tower. The criterion requires the second trigger to be the first certificate of occupancy for any portion of the project, not specifically 100 residential units in the Residential Tower. The definition is therefore narrower and does not match the required formulation.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct fixed rent escalation: 2.5% compounding every 5 years
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.4 includes fixed rent escalations for Rent Years 1–5 at $2,850,000, Years 6–10 at $3,224,500, and Years 11–15 at $3,648,200. These amounts correspond to 2.5% annual compounding over five-year steps, matching the criterion. Although the percentage is not restated in Section 6.4, the required fixed escalation structure and correct calculated amounts are present.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes CPI rent reset mechanism starting Year 16
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains all core elements the criterion requires. Section 1.1 defines 'CPI' as the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, Northeast Region, All Items (Series ID CUUR0100SA0) — i.e., CPI-U Northeast Region. Section 1.1 defines 'Reset Date' as Rent Years 16, 26, 36, 46, 56, 66, 76, 86, and 96, establishing the first reset at Year 16 and subsequent resets every 10 years. Section 6.5 sets Base Rent at each Reset Date to the greater of (a) the pre-reset Base Rent compounded at 2.5% over ten years, or (b) the pre-reset Base Rent adjusted by the ratio of CPI at the reset to CPI at the prior reset (with a 4% annual cap), and prohibits any reduction below the initial Base Rent of $2,850,000. Section 6.6 provides full CPI mechanics (base index, rebasing, successor index). While Section 6.5 applies the CPI adjustment to the Base Rent in effect immediately prior to each Reset Date rather than strictly to the 'initial base rent,' the mechanism still features a running 'greater-of' comparison between the compounded fixed escalation and the CPI adjustment. The essential components of the criterion — a CPI-U (Northeast) reset beginning Year 16, repeating every 10 years, structured as the greater of a compounded fixed escalation or a CPI adjustment — are clearly present and operative, so the output satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct percentage rent terms
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.1 provides Percentage Rent equal to 2.0% of Gross Revenues exceeding the Breakpoint, beginning with Rent Year 6. The Breakpoint is defined in Section 1.1 as $28,500,000 (with indexing under Section 7.5 and a floor at $28.5M), satisfying the 'fixed or indexed' requirement. Section 7.7 requires annual calculation and payment within 90 days after the end of each Rent Year. All three elements of the criterion—rate, commencement year, and payment timing—are correctly stated. Minor interpretive point: the commencement is keyed to 'Rent Year 6' (which begins on the Rent Commencement Date) rather than the calendar 'Lease Year 6,' but this is a coherent and non-material distinction that does not render the terms incorrect under the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct remediation credit of $1,800,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.5(a) sets the Remediation Credit at exactly $1,800,000, and Section 9.5(b) specifies the application mechanism: the first seven full calendar months of Base Rent after the Rent Commencement Date are reduced to $0 (7 × $237,500 = $1,662,500), the eighth month is reduced by $137,500 (Tenant pays $100,000), and full Base Rent resumes in month nine — totaling $1,800,000, i.e., approximately 7.5 months of rent. Section 9.5(c)-(d) add carryforward and cash-payment-on-early-termination protections, and Exhibit H corroborates the credit and cost allocation. The amount and mechanism match the criterion precisely.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit amount and form (LOC)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.1 of the lease requires a Security Deposit of $5,700,000 (expressed as 24 months of the $237,500 initial monthly Base Rent, which computes correctly to $5,700,000), in the form of an irrevocable standby letter of credit substantially in the form of Exhibit J, issued by a commercial bank organized under U.S. or state law with a minimum credit rating of A- from Standard & Poor's or A3 from Moody's Investors Service (or equivalent). Exhibit J reiterates the irrevocable standby LOC form, the beneficiary, the $5,700,000 amount (reducible to $2,850,000), the A-/A3 rating requirement, and draw conditions limited to uncured monetary defaults. The additional option for a cash deposit at Tenant's election does not undercut the required LOC form. The amount, form, and credit rating requirement all match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit reduction mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 10, Section 10.2 provides that the Security Deposit reduces to $2,850,000 upon satisfaction of the Reduction Conditions, which include (a) the Project achieving and maintaining an overall occupancy rate of 90% or greater for 24 consecutive months, (b) delivery of a certification with supporting rent roll data, and (c) no continuing Event of Default. This matches the criterion exactly: reduced amount of $2,850,000 and threshold of 90% occupancy for 24 consecutive months. Section 10.3 further defines occupancy rate, and Section 10.4 specifies the mechanics. The mechanism is present and not materially incorrect.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 1: construction commencement within 18 months (by April 1, 2027)
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly includes Milestone 1 in Section 4.2 (and repeats it in Exhibit I), defining "Commencement of Construction" as the pouring of footings after issuance of building permits, to be achieved within 18 months of the Lease Commencement Date with an Outside Date of April 1, 2027 (based on the assumed October 1, 2025 commencement). The deadline is consistent with an 18-month period and is not materially incorrect.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 2: structural frame within 42 months (by April 1, 2029)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 of the lease expressly includes Milestone 2 — 'Completion of Structural Frame (Residential Tower)' — at 42 months from the Lease Commencement Date, with an Outside Date of April 1, 2029 (assuming the October 1, 2025 commencement). The milestone is defined in Section 4.2(b) as topping-out of the structural steel and/or concrete frame, and is repeated in Exhibit I (Development Milestone Schedule). The milestone is also referenced in Sections 4.5, 5.1, and 19.1(c) (though only Milestones 1 and 3 carry reverter consequences). The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 3: Phase 1 substantial completion within 60 months (by October 1, 2030)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 expressly sets out Development Milestones in a table, with Milestone 3 defined as 'Substantial Completion of Phase 1' at 60 months from the Lease Commencement Date, with an Outside Date of October 1, 2030 (assuming the October 1, 2025 commencement). Section 1.1 defines 'Phase 1' as the Residential Tower and ground-floor retail, and 'Substantial Completion' is defined by reference to issuance of a certificate of occupancy for those components. Exhibit I (Development Milestone Schedule) repeats Milestone 3 at 60 months / October 1, 2030, and Section 4.5 makes failure of Milestone 3 subject to the Reverter Right. The deadline is materially correct and matches the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 4: Phase 2 substantial completion within 84 months (by October 1, 2032)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 of the lease includes a Development Milestones table with Milestone 4 defined as 'Substantial Completion of Phase 2' (the Office Building) at 84 months from the Lease Commencement Date, with an Outside Date of October 1, 2032 (based on the assumed October 1, 2025 commencement). Milestone 4 is also repeated in Exhibit I (Development Milestone Schedule). Although Section 4.5 provides that failure to achieve Milestone 4 is not an Event of Default, the milestone is expressly included with the correct 84-month deadline, which is what the criterion requires.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes force majeure extension provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.3 expressly provides day-for-day force majeure extensions for milestone deadlines, capped at 18 months aggregate, including up to 12 months for force majeure generally and up to 6 additional months for governmental permitting delays. This satisfies the criterion, especially as additional environmental/coastal extensions are also included in Section 4.4 without counting against the cap.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes reverter right provisions for Milestones 1 and 3
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly includes a reverter right. Article 5, Section 5.1 grants Landlord the right, upon Tenant's failure to achieve Milestone 1 or Milestone 3 (as extended under Sections 4.3 and 4.4), to terminate the lease and cause the Premises and Improvements to revert. Section 4.5 confirms this is the sole remedy for Milestone 1/Milestone 3 failures and that Milestone 2/4 failures are not defaults. Section 5.2 provides that upon delivery of a Milestone Default Notice (written notice specifying the milestone and factual basis per Section 5.3), Tenant has 180 days (the 'Milestone Cure Period') to cure before the reverter can be exercised. Thus the reverter right for Milestones 1 and 3, with a 180-day written-notice/cure period, is present. The presence of additional conditions precedent (Leasehold Mortgagee cure period, improvement compensation payment, mediation) provides extra protection but does not negate the required 180-day notice provision.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes leasehold mortgage permission for construction financing
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 17 expressly permits Tenant to grant one or more Leasehold Mortgages encumbering its leasehold estate without Landlord consent, and Recital E ties this to the $285,000,000 construction loan from Bayside Federal Lending Corp. Section 17.1 explicitly allows the mortgage to cover the leasehold estate, improvements, subleases, rents, and to secure collateral assignments, and Sections 17.2–17.13 provide recognition, SNDA, cure, new-lease, and foreclosure rights—satisfying the criterion that the lease permit leasehold mortgage financing for construction.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes SNDA framework with the Authority
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains a comprehensive SNDA framework involving the Authority. Section 2.5(e) makes execution and delivery of the SNDA by Landlord (the Authority) and the Leasehold Mortgagee a condition precedent to the Lease Commencement Date. Section 17.4 expressly requires the Authority to execute and deliver an SNDA substantially in the form of Exhibit E, in form and substance reasonably acceptable to the Leasehold Mortgagee, and enumerates its minimum required contents (acknowledgment of the Leasehold Mortgage's priority, non-disturbance, attornment/recognition of the mortgagee or foreclosure purchaser as tenant without fee, cure and notice rights, New Lease right, prohibition on voluntary surrender/amendment, casualty/condemnation rights). It also obligates the Authority to deliver replacement/amended SNDAs for refinancing lenders within 15 business days without fee. Exhibit E provides the form of SNDA and Exhibit F the mortgagee recognition/new lease agreement, and Sections 5.5(c), 16.5, and 17.12 reference the SNDA for payment direction. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes New Lease right for lender if ground lease is terminated
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly includes a New Lease right in Section 17.5. It allows the Leasehold Mortgagee or its designee to obtain a new ground lease on the same terms if the lease is terminated for any reason, including Tenant default. The cure conditions match the criterion: monetary defaults within 60 days after the New Lease effective date, and non-monetary defaults within 90 days or commencement within 90 days with diligent pursuit thereafter. The right is also reinforced in Sections 17.4, 17.6, and Exhibit F.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires Authority to provide lender copies of default notices
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly requires the Authority/Landlord to deliver copies of all notices, demands, and communications—including default and termination notices—to each Leasehold Mortgagee simultaneously with delivery to Tenant. Sections 17.3, 5.4(a), and 19.3 make delivery to the mortgagee mandatory and even render non-compliant default/termination notices void. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease prohibits voluntary surrender without lender consent
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 17.7 expressly states that, while any Leasehold Mortgage is in effect, Landlord shall not accept a voluntary surrender, cancellation, or termination of the Lease from Tenant without the prior written consent of each Leasehold Mortgagee, and any purported surrender without such consent is void. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes ELUR acknowledgment and compliance obligations
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly acknowledges the ELUR in Recital F, identifying it as recorded March 22, 2018 in Volume 412, Page 88 of the Port Calloway Land Records, and defines it in Article 1 (including 'all activity and use limitations, engineered barrier requirements, and reporting obligations'). Compliance obligations are pervasive: Section 4.7(c) requires construction in compliance with the ELUR; Section 9.3 addresses ELUR compliance and ground-floor use, including Landlord's obligation to obtain a DEEP interpretation/variance; Section 9.6(c) requires Tenant to maintain, inspect, and repair the engineered barrier required by the ELUR, with Landlord bearing costs for pre-existing deficiencies; Section 9.7 imposes ongoing ELUR compliance obligations; and Exhibit H requires reconstruction of the engineered barrier in accordance with the ELUR as part of the remediation scope. The engineered barrier/ground-disturbance requirement is thus both referenced and operationalized.

criteria_results.title: Lease specifies Tenant's remaining remediation responsibility of $600,000
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly allocates remediation costs. Section 9.5(a) provides a Remediation Credit of $1,800,000 against Base Rent, and Section 9.4(c) caps Tenant's aggregate liability for the Tenant Remediation Scope at $600,000 (with any excess over the $2,400,000 aggregate estimate borne by Landlord). Exhibit H confirms the arithmetic: total estimated cost of $2,400,000, less $1,800,000 credit to Landlord, leaving $600,000 as Tenant's share. The allocation is present and the amounts are correct and consistent with the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes comprehensive insurance requirements
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 14 of the lease comprehensively addresses insurance. Section 14.1(a) requires CGL at $10M per occurrence/$20M aggregate; 14.1(c) requires All-Risk (Special Form) property insurance on a full replacement-cost basis and, during construction, builder's risk insurance on a completed-value basis; 14.1(d) requires flood insurance at full replacement cost (plus maximum NFIP coverage); 14.1(e) requires Pollution Legal Liability at $5M per occurrence/$10M aggregate (to the extent commercially available); and 14.1(f) requires Workers' Compensation per Connecticut statute plus employer's liability. Section 14.2 names the Authority (Landlord) and the City as additional insureds on the CGL, umbrella/excess, and environmental policies, and names Landlord as an additional loss payee on the property insurance for its fee interest—the standard analogue to additional-insured status on a property policy. Every enumerated requirement is present; no requirement is missing (let alone more than two). The environmental-coverage carve-out for known conditions (Section 9.9) does not eliminate the requirement, and Section 14.5 adds a periodic review mechanism plus self-insurance conditions in 14.6.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes triple-net structure for taxes and operating costs
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly establishes a triple-net structure: Section 2.1 leases the Premises on a 'triple-net basis'; Section 8.1 states the Lease is intended to be a triple-net ground lease with Tenant paying all Taxes levied against the Premises and Improvements; Section 8.2 defines Taxes broadly to include real property taxes, ad valorem taxes, special/benefit assessments, and sewer/water charges; Article 13 obligates Tenant at its sole cost to maintain, repair, and replace the Premises and Improvements; and Article 14 requires Tenant to carry all property, liability, flood, and environmental insurance at its own cost. The negotiated tax abatement (Section 8.6), remediation credit (Section 9.5), and limited Express Offsets do not change the fundamental allocation—Tenant bears taxes, assessments, insurance, utilities, and operating/maintenance costs, which is consistent with an NNN ground lease.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes tax abatement phase-in schedule
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.6(a) of the lease contains an explicit 15-year tax abatement phase-in schedule with a table: Rent Years 1–5 at 25% of actual assessed value, Years 6–10 at 50%, Years 11–15 at 75%, and 100% thereafter. Section 8.6(b) defines the 15-year Abatement Period commencing on the Rent Commencement Date, and Section 8.6(d) confirms taxes are calculated on actual assessed value and mill rate multiplied by the Applicable Percentage. Exhibit L (Form of Tax Abatement Agreement) also references the same 15-year abatement period and the 25%/50%/75%/100% Applicable Percentages. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes permitted use restrictions consistent with term sheet
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 11.1 expressly permits residential apartments, Class A office, ground-floor retail, restaurants (including liquor service licensed by the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection), and accessory parking, plus ancillary uses. It expressly prohibits adult entertainment establishments, firearms sales, pawnshops, gasoline service stations, and industrial/manufacturing (and warehousing) uses. All required permitted uses and all required excluded uses are present, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires minimum 8,000 SF publicly accessible open space
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.8 of the lease expressly requires Tenant to include "a minimum of eight thousand (8,000) square feet of publicly accessible open space on the waterfront (eastern) side of the Premises, designed, constructed, and maintained by Tenant, and connected to the existing public pedestrian promenade." This matches the criterion precisely, and the requirement is reinforced in Recital D and the definition of the Project.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes assignment/subletting provisions with ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes assignment and subletting provisions in Article 18 and expressly grants the Authority a right of first refusal in Section 18.5 for Transfers to non-affiliated entities during the first 20 years of the Term. The ROFR is subject to exclusions for Permitted Transfers and financing-related transfers, consistent with the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes finished floor elevation requirement of at least 15 ft NAVD88
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.7(b) of the lease expressly requires the Project to be designed and constructed 'with a finished floor elevation of no less than fifteen (15) feet NAVD88, providing not less than three (3) feet of freeboard above the BFE,' consistent with the Recital G reference to BFE of 12 feet NAVD88. This satisfies the criterion's requirement of a finished floor elevation of at least 15 ft NAVD88.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes default and remedies provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 19 of the lease contains comprehensive default and remedies provisions. Section 19.1 defines multiple Tenant Events of Default — monetary default (cured within 10 Business Days after written notice), non-monetary default (30 days after written notice, extendable if cure is diligently pursued), Milestone failure (subject to 180-day Milestone Cure Period and Mortgagee Cure Period), insolvency, abandonment (180 days), and misrepresentation — each with specified notice and cure periods stated in days/months. Section 19.4 defines Landlord Events of Default (failure to perform material obligations, breach of representations, failure to pay amounts due, improper fee transfer) with a 30-day notice/cure period (and 90 days for uncurable-by-30-days defaults under Section 19.5(e)). Section 19.2 and 19.5 set forth the respective remedies, including termination, offset, self-help, specific performance, and damages, with Section 19.3 making notice and cure a condition precedent. This satisfies the criterion of at least two Tenant events of default and at least one Landlord event of default with specified notice and cure periods.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes indemnification provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains multiple indemnification provisions running in Tenant's favor, but it also includes a Tenant indemnity in favor of the Authority: Section 9.4(e) requires Tenant to 'indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Landlord' from all claims, liabilities, losses, damages, penalties, fines, costs, and expenses arising out of any Release of Hazardous Materials at the Premises caused by Tenant's acts or omissions after the Lease Commencement Date (expressly surviving termination under Section 9.4(f)), and Section 8.3 requires Tenant to indemnify Landlord in connection with deferred contested Taxes relating to the Premises. Tenant also bears broad compliance/insurance obligations (Article 11.3, Article 14) that backstop the Authority against third-party claims from Tenant's occupancy. While the draft does not include a standalone general 'use and occupancy' indemnity covering ordinary third-party bodily injury/property damage claims (only the environmental and tax-related Tenant indemnities are spelled out, with reciprocal Authority indemnities in Sections 9.4(d), 11.9, and 3.6), indemnification provisions under which Tenant indemnifies the Authority for claims tied to its use of the Premises are present, so the criterion is met.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes casualty and condemnation provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains Article 15 (Casualty) and Article 16 (Condemnation). Article 15 includes Tenant's obligation to restore/rebuild improvements after a Casualty (Section 15.1), rent abatement during restoration (15.2), and termination rights (15.4–15.5). Article 16 addresses total and partial condemnation, restoration obligations, and a detailed allocation of the condemnation award between Landlord (fee/land value) and Tenant (leasehold, improvements, trade fixtures, business interruption) in Section 16.3, plus separate claims and payment to the Leasehold Mortgagee. Both required elements are present and substantively developed.

criteria_results.title: Memo includes at least three negotiation recommendations identifying counterparty and specific lease provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo contains numerous negotiation recommendations identifying both the counterparty (e.g., Howard Koss, the Authority's counsel, the Authority, Ridgepoint, DEEP, the City) and the specific lease provisions or issues to negotiate. Examples: (1) Part IV.C.1 recommends raising the ROFR mortgagee carve-out with Howard Koss in the transmittal letter, tied to Draft Lease §§18.6, 18.3, 18.5(d)–(e), and §3.10; (2) Part IV.A recommends sending a title objection under Section 3.4 of the Draft Lease to the Issuing Title Company and requesting the Authority confirm the 2012 taking and recorded lot split, with specific conditions precedent §2.5(b)–(c); (3) Part I.5 lists four specific transmittal requests to Howard Koss including conforming Title Exhibit A and recording amendments to the 2019 ROFR and affordable housing declaration; (4) Part IV.O recommends proposing to Howard Koss a joint DEEP ELUR interpretation request within ten business days; and Part VI supplies a 24-item negotiation matrix listing each Term Sheet term, the Draft Lease position, the expected Authority response, and a fallback. Far more than three qualifying recommendations are provided.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes lender's right to foreclose/assign to qualified transferee
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 17.8 ('Foreclosure and Assignment') expressly grants each Leasehold Mortgagee the unconditional right to foreclose the Leasehold Mortgage (judicially, by power of sale, or otherwise), to accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and to assign the lease to a qualified transferee, without Landlord's prior consent and without triggering Transfer consent requirements or the Right of First Refusal (reinforced by Sections 18.1(c), 18.3(c), and 18.5(d)-(e)). Section 18.4 supplies the reasonable objective qualification standards for a 'qualified transferee' (tangible net worth of at least $75,000,000 or $250,000,000 in managed funds for institutional investors, and at least ten years' experience developing/owning/operating comparable mixed-use or multifamily properties). Landlord must recognize the transferee as Tenant and execute reasonably requested assumption documents. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies the construction loan from Bayside Federal
criteria_results.reasoning: Recital E expressly identifies the construction loan from Bayside Federal Lending Corp. in the original principal amount of $285,000,000, and Section 17.3 designates Bayside Federal Lending Corp. as the initial Leasehold Mortgagee with its notice address. Article 17 further permits and protects the construction financing. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Tenant's obligation to comply with affordable housing covenant
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly includes a mandatory affordable housing covenant. Section 4.9 requires that not fewer than 15% of residential dwelling units be designated affordable to households at or below 80% of AMI published by HUD, and Section 11.5(a) repeats and elaborates that requirement, with detailed mechanics for calculation (§11.5(c)), placement/distribution (§11.5(d)), income verification and monitoring (§11.5(e)), and a Regulatory Agreement (Exhibit K). Although the covenant's duration is framed as the 'Affordable Housing Period' (30 years or the lease term, whichever is earlier) rather than the full 99-year term, the criterion's core requirement—a lease provision mandating a minimum 15% of residential units be affordable at or below 80% AMI—is plainly and unambiguously satisfied. The covenant runs with the leasehold and is enforceable against Tenant for a substantial term, so the affordable housing obligation is included in the lease as required.

criteria_results.title: Both deliverable files are produced
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced two distinct deliverables: (1) a comprehensive Ground Lease Agreement (ground-lease-agreement.docx) with 24 Articles and 12 Exhibits, and (2) a separate drafting issues memorandum (drafting-issues-memo.docx) addressed to the client covering issues, conflicts, and gap analysis. Both required deliverable files are present and substantive.
